label.sl: Kupci, ki les naročijo prek spleta

sl: Domači mojstri v petih državah za les v trgovinah DIY porabijo okoli 1,15 milijarde evrov na leto, v regijah v dosegu Straže okoli 280 milijonov. Spletna žaga lahko realno doseže okoli 17 milijonov. V osnovnem scenariju kanal v petem letu ustvari okoli 1,7 milijona evrov prihodkov in okoli 120.000 evrov dobička nad prodajo istega lesa na debelo, pri tem pa porabi le okoli 4 % proizvodnje žage. Kanal DIY je dodaten posel z višjo maržo, ne zamenjava za izvoz.

Prodajna cena je več kot dvakrat višja od vrednosti lesa na debelo, zato je prispevek na naročilo dober. Dobiček pojedo dostava, delo pri majhnih naročilih in pridobivanje kupcev. Prvi dve leti sta zato v izgubi (zagon, ekipa, razvoj trgovine), kumulativno pa se osnovni scenarij izide v petem letu. V modelu je razrez enkrat na teden v paketu, v tujini pa zbirna vožnja do prevzemnih mest namesto posamičnih palet (paleta v Avstrijo stane 158–190 €).

Velikost naročila. Pri 0,3 m³ na naročilo namesto 0,18 m³ se dobiček v petem letu podvoji (na okoli 250.000 €), pri 0,1 m³ ostane kanal v izgubi. Zato načrtovalnik spodbuja celotne projekte in dodatke (peleti, lubje) namesto posameznih letev. Drugi vzvod je strošek novega kupca: vsebine in Skobi pripeljejo kupce brez plačanih oglasov.

Vrednosti blagovne znamke doma, podatkov o tem, kaj kupci res gradijo, prodaje manjšim mizarjem in obrtnikom (B2B), ki bi prišli prek istega kanala, ter morebitnega partnerstva s trgovinami ali delavnicami. Vse to je dodatek k izračunu.
en: DIYers in the five countries spend around €1.15 billion a year on timber in DIY stores, around €280 million in the regions within reach of Straža. An online sawmill can realistically reach around €17 million of that. In the base scenario the channel makes around €1.7 million of revenue in year 5 and around €120,000 of profit over selling the same timber wholesale, using only about 4 % of the mill's output. The DIY channel is extra business with a higher margin, not a replacement for exports.

The selling price is more than twice the wholesale value of the timber, so the contribution per order is healthy. Delivery, labour on small orders and customer acquisition eat into it. The first two years therefore run at a loss (launch, team, building the shop), and the base scenario breaks even cumulatively in year 5. The model cuts in a weekly batch and serves other countries with a consolidated run to pickup points instead of single pallets (a pallet to Austria costs €158–190).

Order size. At 0.3 m³ per order instead of 0.18 m³, year-5 profit doubles (to around €250,000); at 0.1 m³ the channel stays in the red. That is why the planner encourages whole projects and extras (pellets, bark) rather than single battens. The second lever is the cost of a new customer: content and Skobi bring buyers in without paid ads.

The value of a brand at home, data on what buyers really build, sales to small joiners and tradespeople (B2B) who would come through the same channel, and possible partnerships with stores or workshops. All of that comes on top.
